source.title: ACTR: Aligning Thoughts and Responses for Multilingual Safety in Reasoning LLMs
source.authors: Xian-Hui Zhang; Jian Yu; Cheng-Yu Xie; Chen-Hang Cui; Shu-Yi Miao; Pengyang Shao; Yu Zheng; Fei Shen; Tat-Seng Chua

page_placements.theme: Safety interventions can change benign refusal and useful capability

record.tranche_reason: The study uses neuron masking and selective neuron-parameter training, rather than the original fine-tuning or token-position KL methods, and measures resulting safety behavior. These interventions test whether safety behavior depends on a selected subset of neurons.
record.gate_note: The study tests neuron-level localization (V5), not few-example harmful or benign fine-tuning, first-token KL concentration, opening-token or decoding bypasses, why safety is shallow, or spreading safety across response positions. The English-trace substitution result is recorded as a related finding outside the listed versions. TGS and thought-response inconsistency results are not rows because they measure a different mechanism or construct. The main comparison of ACTR with other methods in Table 4 is not extracted; Tables 3, 5, and 6 report the more direct neuron-intervention and neuron-selection results.
record.test_reason: The study ablates a sparse, selected set of attention-projection weight rows and columns (top 3% per layer) in Qwen3-8B and Gemma4-12B-it. It compares this with count- and layer-matched random masking and measures jailbreak ASR (Table 3). That is a different method aimed at V5's question: whether a small set of weights carries safety behaviour. The other versions are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that reasoning LLMs show a think–response safety disconnect in non-high-resource languages, not explained by reasoning-trace content. Masking a sparse set of 'safety think neurons' causally raises ASR beyond matched random masking. ACTR, which updates only those neurons with a thought–response consistency reward, gives the lowest average ASR among the compared methods, generalizes to unseen languages, preserves utility, and keeps benign refusals low. The authors concede the neurons likely mix safety-specific and general reasoning-transfer roles.
record.recipe_differences: Uses matched neuron masking and neuron-selective consistency optimization, rather than harmful/benign example fine-tuning or aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement. The training reward is thought-response consistency, and only parameters associated with selected safety-think neurons are updated.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes differ by model and benchmark: targeted masking has especially large effects for Gemma4-12B-it. The study selects the top p=3% of neurons; it reports that thresholds above 3% sharply degrade general capability, including an MGSM drop of 83.60 for Gemma4-12B-it at p=5.

fits_no_version.finding: Substituting English-derived reasoning traces into NHR prompts barely changes mean MultiJail ASR (-0.40 pp Qwen3-8B, -0.45 pp Gemma4-12B-it).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The multilingual safety gap in reasoning LLMs is not explained by reasoning-trace content.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse RL training of either random or selected neurons cuts ASR by similar amounts. Random-neuron training sharply raises benign refusals on XSTest (4.40→52.00 Qwen3-8B, 4.80→46.80 Gemma4-12B-it); ACTR does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse parameter updates of any neuron set can restore refusal; which neurons are chosen mainly governs over-refusal.

record.problems: The study uses automated judges for ASR and for consistency rewards. The consistency reward measures agreement, not safety: trajectories judged unsafe in both thought and response can receive reward. The reported evidence covers two models and does not establish that the selected neurons are exclusively safety-specific; the authors state that they may also participate in general reasoning transfer. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the extracted results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 thought-response inconsistency rates and TGS results in Figures 3, 4, and 6 were left out because they do not measure any listed version. Table 4's ACTR-versus-method benchmark comparison was left out because it compares the paper's new method with other methods rather than isolating the claim's object; the neuron-selection ablation and refusal results are recorded from Tables 5 and 6. Figure 5's plotted threshold values were not extracted because the text provides only a qualitative description of the plotted sweep, apart from the stated MGSM drop.

untested.parts: No aligned-vs-base per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. The jailbreaks are translated prompts, not opening-token bypasses.

Only attention Q/K/V/O rows and columns selected by a think-on vs think-off contrast are tested. MLP weights, low-rank or safety-specific (harmful vs benign) localization, and non-reasoning models are not tested.
No test of what causes shallowness.
ACTR is not evaluated for depth of safety across response positions or robustness to fine-tuning or prefilling.

missing.what: Masking-threshold sweep: MultiJail ASR after masking at p=1,2,3,5,7% rises roughly 19.05→31.75→51.79→67.62→68.88, with MGSM falling at p>3. This shows dose-response of localization and the capability cost of larger masks. The model is apparently Gemma4-12B-it (51.79 and 7.89 match Table 3); the paper's 'drops by 83.60' wording is ambiguous.
TGS change after targeted vs random masking (mean +0.696 vs -0.045). Mechanism context only; not a rate of the behaviour.

record.verdict_notes: Only the Table 3 masking rows bear on V5; Table 5/6 rows evaluate the study's own training method and are relinked to none. The neurons are selected by a think-on vs think-off contrast on jailbreak queries, not a harmful-vs-benign contrast, so they may not be safety-specific (Appendix H A2). Masking more than 3% degrades MGSM. ASR is judged by GPT-4o; no uncertainty is reported; there are only two models. Neither original source is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples to measure harmful-request compliance.
No ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction-data fine-tuning.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or analysis of whether divergence is concentrated in the first response positions.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-change bypass tests.
Tests selected safety-think-neuron masking and sparse neuron-associated parameter updates, not localization to a specified number of weights or ranks or an exhaustive circuit analysis.
Does not test whether training data or objective causes safety to be shallow across response positions.
ACTR training is evaluated for safety outcomes and TGS, but the study does not measure whether safety is spread beyond the first response tokens or whether such depth persists.

tranche.reason: Mode-contrastive neuron identification and matched masking provide a different method testing whether existing safety behavior depends on a sparse parameter subset.

source_check.notes: The selected set is the per-layer think-on top-3% set minus the think-off top-3% set, not a measured 3% of all model weights; Appendix H acknowledges mixed safety and general reasoning functions.
